frictionVectors.title: European gas bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Italy and other European buyers seek stable Algerian gas supplies while encouraging additional exports and infrastructure investment. Algiers is using long-term contracts and pipeline access to preserve pricing and political autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger pressures Algeria’s borders and complicates its non-interventionist posture. Foreign military competition in the Sahel increases the risk of proxy activity near Algerian territory.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor geopolitical competition
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the Lobito Corridor is expanding Angola’s strategic options but also makes the country a focal point of competition with Chinese infrastructure and mining interests. Control over rail, port, and copper-cobalt flows remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon revenue pressure
frictionVectors.details: Declining production, debt servicing, and dependence on foreign oil operators constrain Luanda’s fiscal sovereignty. New offshore investment is needed, but contract terms and infrastructure requirements limit the state’s bargaining room.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and pipeline tension
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained over border access and the oil export corridor to Benin’s coast. The dispute threatens transit revenue and exposes Cotonou to pressure from neighboring military governments.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal security competition
frictionVectors.details: Benin is receiving growing external security assistance to contain militant spillover from the Sahel. Reliance on foreign training, surveillance, and maritime support could limit independent control of border and port security.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and domestic beneficiation in its diamond partnership with De Beers. The strategy strengthens sovereignty but risks investment delays and market exposure if global diamond demand weakens.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are targeting Botswana’s copper, nickel, and other mineral prospects, while rail, power, and water constraints limit local processing. Gaborone must balance rapid capital inflows against maintaining regulatory and environmental control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty versus investment
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and control over gold production, challenging foreign mining operators and revising contract expectations. Increased nationalization rhetoric may raise revenues but could reduce technical capacity and formal investment.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou’s reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western influence but created a new external dependency. Limited transparency around security arrangements and mining access complicates claims of full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–Burundi Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border destabilization continue to restrict trade and regional cooperation. The dispute also complicates Burundi’s security posture in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater control over nickel and rare-earth development, but financing, processing capacity, and transport corridors remain heavily dependent on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Competition for Port Access
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and other maritime assets attract interest from European, American, and Chinese actors. Praia must balance investment and security partnerships without surrendering strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external tourism demand, imported fuel, and climate-related water stress. Renewable-energy expansion offers greater autonomy but still requires outside capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Projects
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, mining, and major transport projects rely substantially on foreign firms and lenders, limiting domestic value capture despite growing resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict Disrupts Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, plantations, and public infrastructure. Cross-border insecurity around the Far North further strains state control over trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Security-linked foreign actors and informal networks compete for access to gold and diamonds, while weak oversight limits state revenue and local control over extraction.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bangui remains heavily dependent on Russian-linked security support and other external partners to protect the regime and key corridors. This dependence trades short-term security for reduced strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production, export infrastructure, and foreign operators. Price volatility and opaque revenue management constrain the government’s ability to convert resource wealth into broad development.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French Security Recalibration
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown of France’s traditional military role forces N’Djamena to diversify security ties while managing threats from Sudan, Libya, and insurgent networks. External support remains essential to protecting strategic corridors and regime stability.

frictionVectors.title: France and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Mayotte dispute continues to constrain Comorian sovereignty and relations with France. Migration controls and maritime enforcement remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external donors and foreign contractors for ports, energy, and telecommunications. Limited domestic capacity weakens control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain dominated by foreign capital, traders, and processing networks, especially those linked to China. Kinshasa is seeking better terms and local processing but retains limited leverage.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and regional security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in North Kivu continues to challenge state authority and disrupts mineral supply routes. Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of backing armed groups, while regional diplomacy and external mediation remain inconclusive.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy and public finances remain highly exposed to oil production, foreign operators, and price volatility. Domestic value capture and diversification remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and lenders retain a major role in roads, public works, and resource-linked projects. Debt and contract transparency concerns constrain Brazzaville's bargaining autonomy.

highlights: Cocoa reforms seek greater local value

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire remains exposed to foreign buyers and processors despite efforts to raise farm-gate incomes and expand domestic processing. New sustainability rules and market concentration create additional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic port competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion strengthens national and regional autonomy, but foreign shipping, logistics, and financing interests retain substantial influence. Competition with Tema and San Pedro shapes infrastructure decisions.

highlights: Ports remain exposed to external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military basing
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but this creates dependence on external security patrons. Rivalry among these powers increases pressure on national alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Port debt and corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed ports and logistics projects are central to the economy and to Ethiopia's trade access. Debt exposure and disputes over terminal operations limit Djibouti's ability to retain full strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose Ethiopia's unilateral control over Nile flows, viewing the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a strategic threat. Negotiations remain vulnerable to regional escalation and shifting Sudanese alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf Capital and Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Gulf financing supports Egypt's foreign-exchange position and major infrastructure, but acquisitions and development rights around ports and strategic land raise concerns about long-term sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Declining Oil and Gas Output
frictionVectors.details: Falling production is narrowing fiscal space and increasing reliance on foreign operators, technical partners, and opaque hydrocarbons agreements. The state retains formal ownership but has limited leverage over capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Monetization and LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea is seeking regional gas feedstock and new LNG investment to sustain its energy hub. Infrastructure dependence gives external companies substantial influence over the country's remaining export capacity.

highlights: Red Sea Position Gains Strategic Value

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline is increasingly important amid conflict in Sudan and instability around the Red Sea. External military competition could generate revenue and leverage for Asmara while increasing sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects remain central to export earnings but depend heavily on foreign capital and operators. Limited transparency and sanctions exposure complicate efforts to convert mineral wealth into broad domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Southern African Customs Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's trade, customs revenue, electricity links, and supply chains remain deeply tied to South Africa and the wider SACU system. This provides stability but constrains independent fiscal and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The country remains exposed to imported electricity and external financing for major water and transport projects. Delays or financing conditions can limit national control over essential infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Dam Regional Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam improves Ethiopia's potential control over electricity and water infrastructure, but unresolved arrangements with Egypt and Sudan leave the project exposed to diplomatic and security pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on foreign lenders, contractors, and imported technology limit Addis Ababa's room for maneuver. Conflict-related fiscal pressure further increases the influence of external financial partners.

highlights: Military-led transition seeks tighter control of extractives
Manganese and oil remain strategically exposed

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transition government is pressing for greater domestic value addition and oversight of manganese, iron ore, and oil projects. Tensions may rise with foreign operators if contract reviews are perceived as abrupt or politicized.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon relies on foreign capital and expertise for rail, port, and export infrastructure linking mineral production to the coast. This limits the government's practical autonomy despite stronger political control.

highlights: Tourism and remittances anchor a fragile economy
Senegal remains the pivotal external partner

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked transport and security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's geographic dependence on Senegal affects road access, trade corridors, and security cooperation. Periodic border, customs, and fisheries disputes can quickly become politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal resource pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak monitoring threaten local livelihoods and maritime sovereignty. Limited enforcement capacity leaves the sector vulnerable to opaque licensing and external commercial pressure.

highlights: Debt restructuring is reshaping economic sovereignty
Gold remains dominant as lithium and oil attract scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Extractives governance and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages water systems and exposes gaps in state control, while emerging lithium projects raise demands for local processing and transparent contracts. Foreign buyers and domestic political networks remain influential across the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-supported fiscal reforms and debt restructuring constrain policy space, while Chinese and other external lenders retain importance in infrastructure and commodity-linked finance. Ghana is seeking a balance between investment access and reduced dependence.

highlights: Bauxite wealth is expanding without equivalent domestic processing
Simandou could transform regional mineral logistics

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Large bauxite and iron-ore projects are dominated by foreign consortia, leaving Guinea dependent on external capital, technology, and export infrastructure. Government demands for local content and processing continue to collide with project financing realities.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor and political centralization
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou rail, port, and mining complex will deepen Guinea's strategic ties with China and other investors. Concentrated military rule and opaque contracting create risks around revenue management, land access, and regional spillovers.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the core economic lifeline
Political fragility limits control over ports and resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-chain dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's cashew sector, while weak state institutions limit bargaining power. Price shocks and export disruptions can rapidly affect public stability.

frictionVectors.title: Port, narcotics, and maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's limited port and maritime enforcement capacity leaves the country exposed to transnational trafficking and external influence. Dependence on regional security assistance, particularly from Senegal and wider West African partners, constrains sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-linked fiscal reforms with substantial obligations to Chinese and other external lenders. Debt service limits room for fully independent infrastructure and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains strategically vital, while regional competition from Tanzanian and Djiboutian corridors is increasing. Foreign operators and financiers retain influence over transport infrastructure and trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and related infrastructure provide essential revenue but bind national development to South African demand and financing. Delays and cost pressures around the Lesotho Highlands Water Project intensify this asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Manufacturing Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The manufacturing base remains highly dependent on foreign investors, imported inputs, and preferential access to external markets. Shifts in trade preferences or investor strategy can rapidly affect employment and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mineral Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and associated rail and port arrangements give foreign concessionaires substantial influence over Liberia's export economy. Domestic value addition and state bargaining power remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Concession Governance Risk
frictionVectors.details: The government faces pressure to attract investment while tightening oversight of mining, forestry, and maritime assets. Weak institutional capacity leaves contracts and infrastructure vulnerable to unequal bargaining and rent leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Assets
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest authority over production, export terminals, and budget flows. Periodic blockades and production disruptions expose the limits of national control over the hydrocarbon sector.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security partnerships, mercenary networks, and competing diplomatic patrons continue to shape Libya's political settlement. External actors also seek preferential access to energy, reconstruction, and port opportunities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export networks. Madagascar captures revenue but retains limited control over processing, pricing, and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak transport links constrain domestic industrialization and increase dependence on external project finance. Mining enclaves can therefore remain commercially viable without generating broad sovereign resource security.

frictionVectors.title: IMF Reform and External Financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms are narrowing fiscal autonomy while Malawi remains vulnerable to donor and creditor conditions. Foreign-exchange shortages continue to restrict fuel, fertilizer, and industrial imports.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence Risk
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium and rare-earth projects could improve export earnings but may reproduce enclave-style extraction if contract transparency, local processing, and environmental safeguards remain weak.

highlights: Gold sector faces competing external pressures

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The ruling junta relies heavily on Russian security partnerships while reducing cooperation with Western and regional actors. This may preserve regime security but increases opaque political and commercial concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Mining Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking greater state control and revenue from gold, bringing it into sharper disputes with foreign mining companies. Insecurity and weak regulatory capacity limit the benefits reaching the broader economy.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential but exposes Mauritania to foreign operators, export infrastructure constraints, and cross-border governance risks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals and Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in iron ore, ports, railways, and proposed green-hydrogen projects could diversify the economy. Weak local value addition and dependence on external capital remain persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago is advancing diplomatically, but the future of the Diego Garcia military facility remains tied to negotiations with the United Kingdom and the United States.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius seeks to expand as an Indian Ocean logistics and financial hub while balancing ties with India, China, Gulf investors, and Western partners. Port development could create strategic dependence if financing and security arrangements become concentrated.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate assets, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy projects in Western Sahara to consolidate territorial control. Foreign commercial and diplomatic support remains vulnerable to legal and political disputes over the territory's status.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large investments in solar power, desalination, and green hydrogen strengthen resource sovereignty, but the country remains exposed to drought, imported energy inputs, and foreign technology and financing.

highlights: LNG momentum returns under heavy security dependence
Cabo Delgado remains a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security and LNG enclaves
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and external security partners remain central to protecting Cabo Delgado gas infrastructure, limiting Maputo's autonomous control over the project zone.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent disruption of northern corridors
frictionVectors.details: Islamist insurgency continues to threaten transport, agricultural activity, and state access in the north, despite improved protection around strategic LNG assets.

highlights: Oil and green-hydrogen bets reshape sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic discoveries
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate capital and technical capacity in offshore oil, uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen projects, creating pressure for stronger local-content and revenue safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Water and power constraints
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen and mining projects face scarce water, grid limitations, and transport bottlenecks that could leave Namibia dependent on external infrastructure finance.

highlights: Junta tightens control over extractive assets
Security partnerships pivot away from the West

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and oil renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control and value capture from uranium and oil while confronting foreign operators over licenses, ownership, and operating terms.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security and export isolation
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence, strained regional relations, and reliance on alternative external security partners threaten roads, pipelines, and dependable export access.

highlights: Oil reform advances amid persistent insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and production decline
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs international finance and technology to reverse mature-field decline, while contract uncertainty, crude theft, and regulatory disputes weaken bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and grid vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Attacks, sabotage, and weak transmission infrastructure continue to constrain oil evacuation, gas expansion, and reliable domestic power supply.

highlights: Mineral processing ambitions confront regional war

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo mineral scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda-linked networks benefit from eastern DRC mineral flows continue to generate diplomatic pressure, sanctions risk, and sovereignty disputes.

frictionVectors.title: External security and aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Kigali's security partnerships and donor relationships provide strategic capacity but expose the country to conditionality, reputational costs, and shifting foreign priorities.

highlights: Maritime security and fisheries are strategic priorities

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea resource competition
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe has valuable maritime space but limited capacity to monitor illegal fishing, offshore licensing, and environmental risks. External security and commercial partners therefore retain significant influence over its blue economy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country remains dependent on external financing and contractors for ports, electricity, roads, and digital connectivity. This constrains bargaining power even as the government seeks to diversify partners.

highlights: Sovereignty-first economic policy faces financing pressure

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract control
frictionVectors.details: Production from the Sangomar field and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers Senegal greater resource leverage, but foreign operators, financing structures, and revenue-management rules remain central to the gains captured domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stress and scrutiny of previously contracted projects limit Dakar's room to rapidly renegotiate external obligations. Relations with international lenders and infrastructure partners are becoming a core sovereignty constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances security, investment, and maritime cooperation among India, China, Western partners, and Gulf actors. Its small territory and exclusive economic zone make port access and surveillance politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and environmental sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and climate impacts challenge the state's ability to secure long-term value from its maritime zone. Conservation-finance arrangements improve capacity but can also attach external policy conditions.

highlights: Mining investment is expanding state revenues
Resource nationalism is testing investor confidence

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects bring badly needed foreign capital but leave Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and external operators. The government's push for higher local value capture and stronger fiscal terms risks disputes with investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors, port capacity, electricity, and transport infrastructure remain dependent on foreign finance and technical partners. This limits the country's ability to convert mineral wealth into broad domestic industrial capacity.

highlights: Fragmented authority weakens national bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil and licensing competition
frictionVectors.details: Mogadishu is promoting offshore petroleum licensing, but disputed federal and regional authority, weak regulation, and limited maritime enforcement create openings for external companies and political patrons to shape the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and regional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Gulf, and neighboring-state involvement in ports and security infrastructure intersects with tensions involving Somaliland and Ethiopia. These arrangements can improve connectivity while diluting a coherent national approach to maritime sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and rail bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, port congestion, and rail failures reduce state control over mineral exports and strengthen pressure from mining investors and private infrastructure operators.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals, while Pretoria seeks non-alignment and domestic beneficiation.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to regional war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving national revenue and production vulnerable to fighting, sabotage, and bargaining by Sudanese and foreign intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented security patronage
frictionVectors.details: Political elites remain dependent on external mediation, arms networks, and neighboring states, limiting sovereign control over oil fields, transport corridors, and public finances.

highlights: Gold and ports draw competing patrons

frictionVectors.title: Externalized gold economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks finance rival armed actors and attract regional buyers, weakening civilian oversight and diverting strategic revenues beyond formal state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated maritime facilities are exposed to competition among Gulf, regional, and global powers seeking influence over trade routes, military access, and reconstruction contracts.

highlights: Ports and corridors are gaining strategic weight
Critical-minerals policy is becoming more assertive

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors are attracting Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western interest, creating leverage but also pressure over concessions, financing, and operating control.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-nationalism balancing act
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns from gold, graphite, and nickel while managing investor concerns over licensing terms and regulatory predictability.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port influence competition
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to coastal and Sahel trade, drawing sustained interest from European, Chinese, Turkish, and Gulf-linked commercial networks that can shape infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover and phosphate control
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent pressure near northern borders raises security costs, while phosphate extraction and associated logistics remain vulnerable to opaque contracting and unequal distribution of resource gains.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financial Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European support on migration, trade, and financing gives Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Debt constraints limit Tunis's room to reject externally shaped economic conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported gas and electricity, while delayed renewable and grid investment weakens its energy sovereignty. Regional interconnection projects could improve resilience but also increase dependence on external financing.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: The EACOP pipeline and upstream oil projects promise major state revenue but leave Uganda dependent on foreign capital, technology, and export infrastructure. Environmental litigation and displacement concerns continue to generate international pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, energy, and industrial construction, creating financing and procurement dependencies. Kampala is seeking greater local participation while managing repayment pressure and strategic bargaining risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Copper remains the backbone of Zambia's fiscal and export position, but production and processing are still heavily shaped by multinational investors. Disputes over taxation, royalties, and ownership continue to test the government's ability to capture more value.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Investor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor and competing Chinese, Gulf, and Western investment initiatives are expanding Zambia's infrastructure options. They also risk turning logistics access and mineral supply chains into instruments of external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and beneficiation rules to retain more value from lithium and other minerals, but Chinese and other foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and market access. Weak regulatory capacity limits effective domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Currency Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and persistent currency instability raise operating costs and encourage minerals to be traded through externally controlled channels. Sanctions, restricted finance, and arrears further narrow Harare's infrastructure choices.
